content_html:
One line of evidence that AI might lead to explosive economic growth is the precedent set by the Industrial Revolution. For hundreds of years — 1252 to 1652, to be precise — the compound annual growth rate of per capita real GDP in the UK was around 0.07%. It then began to accelerate, settling into a new compound rate of around 1.02% per year by 1850, which it held until 1913. In other words, growth accelerated by roughly 15 times before; the argument goes that this should make us humble about predicting it can’t happen again, and perhaps we should be open to accelerations of 10 times or more today.

I think this argument is overstated and the analogy between a 10× acceleration today and the acceleration that occurred during the Industrial Revolution is misleading. The goal of the first part of this post is to provide evidence for two claims:

  1. At the outset of the Industrial Revolution, annual growth that was 10× the long-run average was relatively common.
  2. In the contemporary world, annual growth that is 10× the long-run average for the world is much more rare.

The second part of this post characterizes the acceleration that occurred during the Industrial Revolution in terms of the standard deviation of year-to-year variation in growth rates. Applying the same approach to contemporary growth suggests that an IR-style acceleration would take growth in frontier economies to around 2.8% per year — meaningfully faster than today, but well below the 10× claim that is often advanced.

Why go through this exercise? A common reaction to claims that AI will lead to annual growth rates in excess of 20% per year is skepticism and incredulity — it would be so far outside historical experience. A common retort is that the same incredulity would have been wrong in the 1700s: had someone been told that future growth would be 10× the average and dismissed it, they would have made an error.

The goal here is to rescue that initial reaction. A 10x acceleration today is not the same thing as a 10x acceleration in 1700. A person living in the 1700s would have been asked to envision good years becoming much more common — a rate they had already experienced many times. A person today is being asked to envision a qualitatively different kind of economic dynamics, one that falls several standard deviations outside norm for the world today.

All estimates use the Maddison Project Database 2023, which reports GDP per capita in 2011 USD and population in thousands. The final section considers some objections to the relevancy of this analysis.

How common was 10× faster growth in the pre-IR UK?

We will start by establishing that it was quite common for growth to exceed 10× the long-run average in the UK prior to the Industrial Revolution. Over 1252–1652, the long-run average was 0.30% per year. The compound growth rate over this period — the rate at which wealth actually accumulated across generations — was around 0.07% per year. Roughly 10× this compound rate — around 0.66% per year — was exceeded in about 46% of years. (This figure is not sensitive to the exact window chosen: the compound growth rate ranges from 0.07% to 0.18% across plausible alternative start and end years, and the share of years exceeding 10× that rate ranges from about 40% to 50%.)

Distribution of annual GDP per capita growth for the UK, 1252–1652. The dashed red line marks 10× the compound growth rate (0.66%/yr). About 46% of years exceeded this threshold.

Economic statistics from hundreds of years in the past, before we had statistical offices, are of course highly unreliable, and so the rest of this section will try to provide alternative evidence that 10× faster growth was probably reasonably common. First, to eliminate the importance of year-to-year fluctuations, we can focus on 20-year compound average growth rates. The mean compound rate across all 20-year windows is 0.06% per year, consistent with the full-period CAGR of 0.07%, so 10× that is a threshold of around 0.6%. About 17% of 20-year windows exceeded it. If this data is to be believed, it implies that generation-long runs of 10× faster growth were not unheard of prior to the Industrial Revolution.

Distribution of 20-year compound annual GDP per capita growth rates for the UK, 1272–1652. The dashed red line marks 10× the long-run average (0.60%/yr). About 17% of 20-year periods exceeded this threshold.

Our second robustness check is to look for similar patterns over 1960–2022 for countries with characteristics similar to the pre-IR UK. We are assuming that the growth dynamics of this set of contemporary countries is a reasonable analogue for the growth dynamics of the pre-IR UK — and hoping that the data for these modern countries is more reliable than reconstructions of pre-IR UK real GDP per capita.

We identify this set of countries based on GDP per capita, population, and long-run average growth rate. In the Maddison data, pre-IR UK real GDP per capita ranged from $995 to $2,056 (2011 USD), and population data available for 1500 and 1600 shows a range of 3.9 to 6.2 million, with arithmetic mean growth averaging 0.30% per year. We identify countries with real GDP per capita between $800 and $2,500, population between 1 million and 10 million, and average growth between −0.3% and 0.9%. Eight countries satisfy these conditions: Benin, Burundi, Chad, Haiti, Senegal, Sierra Leone, Togo, and Zimbabwe. Their average compound growth rate is 0.35%/yr, and 10× that — around 3.5% per year — was exceeded in about 19% of country-years. This again suggests it was likely the case in the pre-IR UK that annual growth rates exceeding 10× the average were relatively common.

Distribution of annual GDP per capita growth for 8 modern analogue countries (Benin, Burundi, Chad, Haiti, Senegal, Sierra Leone, Togo, Zimbabwe), 1960–2022. The dashed red line marks 10× the average compound growth rate (3.5%/yr). About 19% of country-years exceeded this threshold.

Our final analysis draws on the entire contemporary dataset. The chart below bins all countries in the Maddison data by their 1950–1985 baseline growth rate and shows what share of each group had at least one year between 1986 and 2022 in which growth exceeded 10× that baseline. Countries with zero or negative baseline growth are excluded.

Share of countries in each baseline-growth bin (1950–1985 average) that had at least one year of growth exceeding 10× their baseline during 1986–2022. n gives the number of countries in each bin.

Among the slowest-growing economies — those averaging 0–1%/yr, the same range as our analogues — 94% experienced at least one 10× year. That share falls to 22% for countries averaging 1–2%/yr and to essentially zero above 2%/yr. We find that 10× faster growth is much more common for slow-growing countries, suggesting that a slow-growing economy like the pre-IR UK likely had many years in which growth exceeded 10× its long-run average.

How common is 10× faster growth today?

Imagine living in Britain around 1700, on the eve of the Industrial Revolution. Annual GDP per capita growth had averaged around 0.07% for the past several centuries — but your experience was not of slow, steady progress. Harvest failures, wars, and disease sent annual growth swinging by 10 percentage points or more in either direction. A year of 0.66% growth — ten times the compound growth rate — was not at all unusual: about one year in two already exceeded that threshold. If someone had told you that growth was about to permanently accelerate tenfold, the new rate would have been something you had already lived through many times. It would have felt, year to year, like a run of good harvests.

Today the story is very different. In the contemporary USA, 10× the compound growth rate implies annual growth of roughly 19% per year. Looking only at the experience of Americans living today, they have never experienced this level of growth, even for a single year.

What if we broaden our aperture to the whole world? Below is a histogram of the annual growth rates of all countries in the Maddison dataset from 1950–2022. Only 0.76% of country-years have experienced annual growth rates in excess of 19%.

Distribution of annual GDP per capita growth rates across all countries in the Maddison database, 1950–2022. The dashed red line marks 18.9%/yr — 10× the modern frontier compound growth rate. About 0.8% of country-years exceeded this threshold.

It is worth examining the 89 country-years that did exceed 20%. The large majority fall into two categories that offer no meaningful precedent for an AI-driven acceleration. The first is oil and resource windfalls: Kuwait’s GDP per capita rose 105% in 1992 as oil production restarted after the Gulf War; Libya appears repeatedly through the 1960s oil boom and again in 2012 after Gaddafi fell; Equatorial Guinea, Qatar, Oman, Nigeria, and Gabon each have years driven by commodity discoveries or price spikes. The second is post-conflict recovery: Lebanon in multiple years through its civil war and aftermath, Bosnia in 1996, Rwanda in 1995, Afghanistan in 2002, Iraq in 2004. These are cases of GDP returning to a level it had previously reached, not of an economy operating in a new gear.

A third, smaller category is more interesting: a handful of countries — South Korea in 1953, Botswana in the early 1970s, some Soviet-bloc countries in the early 1950s — achieved brief periods of very fast growth from genuinely low starting points during early industrialization. This category is worth taking seriously as a partial analogue for the AI argument. If AI unlocks a fundamentally new production frontier, one might argue that today’s economies are “at a low base” relative to that frontier’s potential, just as early industrializing economies were relative to the technology they were adopting. I think this is the strongest version of the IR-as-precedent argument.

In sum, a 10× growth acceleration in the contemporary world, even for a single year, would feel qualitatively different from almost all lived experience. It would be a new way for the economy to operate. In contrast, during the Industrial Revolution, a 10× acceleration would feel like a rather ordinary good year for the economy — with the main difference being that these good years would keep on coming.

The standard deviation approach

Suppose we understand the Industrial Revolution as “more of the good years, fewer of the bad years.” What would that feel like today?

If we want to capture what an IR-level acceleration would feel like today relative to our lived experience, we need a ruler calibrated to current growth experience. The standard deviation of annual growth rates is a useful measure here. For reference, the standard deviations across various samples are:

Sample Annual SD
Pre-IR UK, 1252–1652 6.9%
Modern analogue countries (8 countries, 1960–2022) 5.5%
USA, 1950–2022 2.3%
All countries, 1950–2022 6.2%

Using the pre-IR UK data, the Industrial Revolution amounted to an increase in the compound growth rate from 0.07% to 1.02% — a 15× acceleration, not 10×. In terms of standard deviations of annual growth rates, going from 0.07% to 1.02% represents an increase of about 0.14 standard deviations measured against the pre-IR UK annual distribution, or 0.17 standard deviations measured against the modern analogue countries.

Taking the US compound growth rate of 1.9% per year as the frontier baseline, a similarly sized increase — 0.17 standard deviations of the analogue distribution, our preferred measure since it doesn’t rely on the reliability of pre-IR UK data — would take growth to about 2.8% per year. Using the US standard deviation instead gives about 2.3% per year; using the all-country standard deviation gives about 3.0%. For comparison, a genuine 10× increase in the compound growth rate — from 1.9% to 18.9% — would be an increase of 3.1 standard deviations using the analogue SD, or 7.5 standard deviations using the US SD.

Some potential objections and replies

Objection 1: Pre-industrial growth and industrial growth have different mechanisms

One objection might argue that this analysis is irrelevant because the mechanisms underlying annual growth fluctuations in pre-industrial societies (such as weather, disease, and war) are different from the drivers of growth in the industrial world. The very long-run trend strips out irrelevant year-to-year fluctuations, and leaves behind the portion of growth derived from technological progress. This component does accelerate 15x during the Industrial Revolution, and hence provides a precedent for a similar technologically driven acceleration today.

As a response, note that the processes governing economic growth are only incompletely understood. An economy’s technology is certainly an important determinant of the ultimate level of output per person in an economy, but the rate of change at which output per person grows may be limited by many additional factors beyond the speed of technological progress. The rate of change of the economy, for example, might be governed in part by the rate of technological progress, but also by:

  • The ease or difficulty of transferring property rights over productive assets to their most efficient users
  • The propensity of workers to trade income for reductions in hours worked
  • Savings rates and the maturity of financial markets that direct those savings towards productive investment
  • Security of property rights for prosperous economic agents
  • The size of common markets And so on. Importantly, these factors may govern the speed at which it is possible for an economy to grow in both the pre-industrial and industrial eras.

Given the incompleteness of our understanding, it is informative to look at historical precedent. If someone were to argue that a new policy, for example, would increase the growth rate from x to y, it is an informative exercise to ask how often we have seen growth reach y in the past.

Objection 2: Sensitivity to the definition of interval

Another object points out that there is nothing special about a one-year interval. The post establishes that we get different results if we choose to measure growth over one year, 20 years, or a 100+ years. Given there is no reason to privilege one temporal frame over another, we don’t learn much from this exercise.

I disagree; shorter intervals are useful precisely because if we cannot hit a given growth rate on even a very short time interval, it becomes less likely we will hit it on a longer one. Imagine two runners who need to qualify for a race by running a 1600m race in under five minutes. If one of the runners has shown themselves capable of running 400m in well under 75 seconds at least some of the time, they have better odds of running a five minute mile than a runner who has never run 400m in under 75 seconds.

Put another way, the Industrial Revolution’s long-run growth acceleration did not require the UK economy to hit unusually fast short-run growth rates by its own standards, but to hit them more often than it previously did. Explosive growth today would require hitting short-run growth rates that are unusually fast by contemporary standards.

A closing observation

To close, I’ll note that the Industrial Revolution is not the only precedent for a radical growth acceleration. One could point to earlier accelerations, such as the increase in growth rates with the onset of the agricultural revolution, or point to evidence of a generalized tendency for growth to accelerate over human history. We don’t have good economic data from the time of the agricultural revolution, so there wouldn’t need to be much volatility in year-to-year growth during the pre-agricultural era of humanity for growth rates in excess of 0.06% per year to be very common. This would imply that earlier accelerations were also well inside the distribution that had been observed in the past.

In other words, just as the Industrial Revolution was characterized by relatively common “good years” becoming more common and “bad years” becoming less common, so too was the agricultural revolution probably characterized more by “good years” becoming more common, relative to bad years. In neither case did short run growth rates probably surprise their contemporary observers by dramatically accelerating relative to precedents at the time.

The full code and data are in the growth-acceleration repository.

pip install pandas numpy matplotlib openpyxl

Python 3.9+.

Generating the charts

python3 analysis.py

blocks.html_en: We will start by establishing that it was quite common for growth to exceed 10× the long-run average in the UK prior to the Industrial Revolution. Over 1252–1652, the long-run average was 0.30% per year. The compound growth rate over this period — the rate at which wealth actually accumulated across generations — was around 0.07% per year. Roughly 10× this compound rate — around 0.66% per year — was exceeded in about 46% of years. (This figure is not sensitive to the exact window chosen: the compound growth rate ranges from 0.07% to 0.18% across plausible alternative start and end years, and the share of years exceeding 10× that rate ranges from about 40% to 50%.)

blocks.html_en: Economic statistics from hundreds of years in the past, before we had statistical offices, are of course highly unreliable, and so the rest of this section will try to provide alternative evidence that 10× faster growth was probably reasonably common. First, to eliminate the importance of year-to-year fluctuations, we can focus on 20-year compound average growth rates. The mean compound rate across all 20-year windows is 0.06% per year, consistent with the full-period CAGR of 0.07%, so 10× that is a threshold of around 0.6%. blocks.html_en: Imagine living in Britain around 1700, on the eve of the Industrial Revolution. Annual GDP per capita growth had averaged around 0.07% for the past several centuries — but your experience was not of slow, steady progress. Harvest failures, wars, and disease sent annual growth swinging by 10 percentage points or more in either direction. A year of 0.66% growth — ten times the compound growth rate — was not at all unusual: about one year in two already exceeded that threshold. If someone had told you that growth was about to permanently accelerate tenfold, the new rate would have been something you had already lived through many times. It would have felt, year to year, like a run of good harvests.

blocks.html_en: It is worth examining the 89 country-years that did exceed 20%. The large majority fall into two categories that offer no meaningful precedent for an AI-driven acceleration. The first is oil and resource windfalls: Kuwait’s GDP per capita rose 105% in 1992 as oil production restarted after the Gulf War; Libya appears repeatedly through the 1960s oil boom and again in 2012 after Gaddafi fell; Equatorial Guinea, Qatar, Oman, Nigeria, and Gabon each have years driven by commodity discoveries or price spikes. The second is post-conflict recovery: Lebanon in multiple years through its civil war and aftermath, Bosnia in 1996, Rwanda in 1995, Afghanistan in 2002, Iraq in 2004. content_html_zh:
工业革命开创的先例是人工智能可能带来爆炸性经济增长的证据之一。 数百年来——准确地说是1252年至1652年——英国人均实际GDP的年复合增长率约为0.07%。 然后开始加速，到 1850 年新的复合利率稳定在每年 1.02% 左右，并一直保持到 1913 年。 换句话说，增长速度大约是之前的15倍；有人认为，这应该让我们谦虚地预测这种情况不会再次发生，也许我们今天应该对 10 倍或更多的加速持开放态度。

我认为这个论点被夸大了，今天 10 倍的加速度与工业革命期间发生的加速度之间的类比是误导性的。 这篇文章第一部分的目标是为两个主张提供证据：

  1. 在工业革命开始时，年增长率是长期平均水平的 10 倍是相对常见的。
  2. 在当今世界，年增长率达到世界长期平均水平 10 倍的情况更为罕见。

本文的第二部分用增长率逐年变化的标准差来描述工业革命期间发生的加速。 将同样的方法应用于当代增长表明，IR 式的加速将使前沿经济体的增长达到每年 2.8% 左右——明显快于今天，但远低于通常提出的 10 倍的说法。

为什么要进行这个练习？ 对于人工智能将带来超过 20% 的年增长率这一说法，人们普遍的反应是怀疑和怀疑——这远远超出了历史经验。 一个常见的反驳是，同样的怀疑在 1700 年代也是错误的：如果有人被告知未来的增长将是平均水平的 10 倍并予以否认，他们就会犯一个错误。

这里的目标是挽救最初的反应。 今天的 10 倍加速与 1700 年的 10 倍加速不是一回事。 生活在 1700 年代的人会被要求想象美好的岁月会变得更加普遍——他们已经多次经历过这样的情况。 今天，人们被要求设想一种性质不同的经济动态，这种经济动态比当今世界的正常水平下降了几个标准差。

所有估算均使用麦迪逊项目数据库 2023，该数据库报告了 2011 年的人均 GDP（美元）和人口（以千计）。 最后一部分考虑了对此分析的相关性的一些反对意见。

在前 IR 时期的英国，增长 10 倍有多常见？

我们首先要确定的是，在工业革命之前，英国的经济增长超过长期平均水平 10 倍是很常见的。 1252 年至 1652 年期间，长期平均每年为 0.30%。 这段时期的复合增长率（财富在代际间实际积累的速度）约为每年 0.07%。 大约 10 倍的复合率——每年约 0.66%——在大约 46% 的年份里被超过。 （这个数字对所选择的具体窗口并不敏感：在可能的替代起始年和结束年中，复合增长率的范围从 0.07% 到 0.18%，超过 10 倍的年份比例范围从大约 40% 到 50%。）

英国人均 GDP 年增长率分布，1252 年至 1652 年。 红色虚线标记 10 倍复合增长率（0.66%/年）。 大约 46% 的年份超过了这个阈值。

在我们还没有统计局之前，过去数百年的经济统计数据当然非常不可靠，因此本节的其余部分将尝试提供替代证据，证明 10 倍的快速增长可能是相当普遍的。 首先，为了消除逐年波动的重要性，我们可以关注20年复合平均增长率。 所有 20 年窗口的平均复合率为每年 0.06%，与 0.07% 的全期复合年增长率一致，因此 10 倍即 0.6% 左右的阈值。 大约 17% 的 20 年期窗口超过了该值。 如果这些数据可信，则意味着在工业革命之前，一代人的增长速度提高 10 倍并非闻所未闻。

我们的第二项稳健性检查是寻找 1960 年至 2022 年具有与前 IR 英国相似特征的国家的类似模式。 我们假设这组当代国家的增长动态与前IR时期英国的增长动态是合理的类比，并希望这些现代国家的数据比IR前英国实际人均GDP的重建更可靠。

我们根据人均国内生产总值、人口和长期平均增长率来确定这组国家。 在麦迪逊的数据中，IR前的英国实际人均GDP范围为995美元至2,056美元（2011年美元），1500年和1600年的人口数据显示范围为3.9至620万，算术平均增长率为每年0.30%。 我们确定了人均实际 GDP 在 800 美元到 2,500 美元之间、人口在 100 万到 1000 万之间、平均增长率在 -0.3% 到 0.9% 之间的国家。 八个国家满足这些条件：贝宁、布隆迪、乍得、海地、塞内加尔、塞拉利昂、多哥和津巴布韦。 它们的平均复合增长率为每年 0.35%，大约 19% 的国家/地区年复合增长率是其 10 倍（约每年 3.5%）。 这再次表明，在前IR时期的英国，年增长率超过平均水平10倍的情况可能是相对常见的。

如今 10 倍的增长速度有多常见？

想象一下 1700 年左右生活在英国，即工业革命前夕。 过去几个世纪里，人均 GDP 年均增长率约为 0.07%，但你们的经历并不是缓慢、稳定的进步。 收成歉收、战争和疾病导致年增长率向任一方向波动 10 个百分点或更多。 一年 0.66% 的增长率（复合增长率的十倍）一点也不罕见：大约两年中就有一年超过了这一阈值。 如果有人告诉你经济增长将永久加速十倍，那么你可能已经经历过很多次这种新的速度。 年复一年，感觉就像连年丰收。

今天的故事却大不相同了。 在当代美国，10 倍的复合增长率意味着每年大约 19% 的年增长率。 仅看当今美国人的经历，他们从未经历过这种水平的增长，哪怕是一年。

值得研究一下确实超过 20% 的 89 个国家/地区年。 绝大多数属于两类，它们没有为人工智能驱动的加速提供有意义的先例。 首先是石油和资源的横财：1992年，随着海湾战争后石油生产的重新启动，科威特的人均GDP增长了105%；利比亚在 20 世纪 60 年代石油繁荣时期反复出现，并在 2012 年卡扎菲倒台后再次出现；赤道几内亚、卡塔尔、阿曼、尼日利亚和加蓬多年来都受到大宗商品发现或价格飙升的推动。 第二个是冲突后恢复：黎巴嫩经历了内战和战后多年，波斯尼亚1996年，卢旺达1995年，阿富汗2002年，伊拉克2004年。 这些都是国内生产总值恢复到之前达到的水平的情况，而不是经济以新的方式运行的情况。

第三个较小的类别更有趣：少数国家——1953 年的韩国、1970 年代初的博茨瓦纳、1950 年代初的一些苏联集团国家——在早期工业化期间从真正的低起点实现了短暂的非常快速的增长。 作为人工智能论点的部分类比，这一类别值得认真对待。 如果人工智能开启了一个全新的生产前沿，人们可能会认为，相对于该前沿的潜力，当今的经济体“基础较低”，就像早期工业化经济体相对于它们所采用的技术而言一样。 我认为这是 IR 先例论证的最有力版本。

总之，当代世界 10 倍的增长加速，即使是一年，也会与几乎所有的生活经历产生质的不同。 这将是经济运行的新方式。 相比之下，在工业革命期间，10 倍的加速对于经济来说就像是一个相当普通的好年景——主要的区别在于这些好年景会不断到来。

标准差法

假设我们将工业革命理解为“更多的美好岁月，更少的糟糕岁月”。 今天会是什么感觉？

如果我们想要捕捉到相对于我们的生活经历而言，IR 级别的加速在今天的感觉，我们需要一把根据当前成长经历进行校准的标尺。 年增长率的标准差在这里是一个有用的衡量标准。 作为参考，不同样本的标准差为：

样本 年度标准差
前红外英国，1252–1652 6.9%
现代模拟国家（8 个国家，1960–2022） 5.5%
USA, 1950–2022 2.3%
所有国家，1950–2022 6.2%

根据英国前IR数据，工业革命意味着复合增长率从0.07%提高到1.02%——加速了15倍，而不是10倍。 就年增长率的标准差而言，从 0.07% 到 1.02% 意味着与前 IR 英国年度分布相比增加了约 0.14 个标准差，或者与现代类似国家相比增加了 0.17 个标准差。

以美国每年 1.9% 的复合增长率作为前沿基线，类似规模的增长（模拟分布的 0.17 个标准差，我们的首选衡量标准，因为它不依赖于预IR英国数据的可靠性）将使每年增长约 2.8%。 使用美国标准差则得出每年约 2.3%；使用全国标准差得出的结果约为 3.0%。 相比之下，复合增长率真正增长 10 倍——从 1.9% 到 18.9%——使用模拟 SD 时将增加 3.1 个标准差，或使用美国 SD 时增加 7.5 个标准差。

一些潜在的反对意见和答复

反对意见一：前工业化增长和工业化增长有不同的机制

一种反对意见可能会认为这种分析是无关紧要的，因为前工业社会年增长波动的机制（例如天气、疾病和战争）与工业世界的增长驱动因素不同。 超长期趋势剔除了不相关的逐年波动，并留下了技术进步带来的增长部分。 该组件在工业革命期间确实加速了 15 倍，因此为当今类似的技术驱动加速提供了先例。

作为回应，请注意，人们对经济增长的控制过程还没有完全了解。 经济体的技术无疑是经济体中人均产出最终水平的重要决定因素，但人均产出增长的变化速度可能会受到技术进步速度之外的许多其他因素的限制。 例如，经济变化率可能部分取决于技术进步率，但也受以下因素影响：

  • 将生产性资产的产权转移给最有效的使用者的难易程度
  • 工人用收入换取工作时间减少的倾向
  • 储蓄率和金融市场的成熟度将这些储蓄引导至生产性投资
  • 繁荣经济主体的产权保障
  • 共同市场的规模等等。 重要的是，这些因素可能会影响前工业时代和工业时代经济增长的速度。

鉴于我们理解的不完整，看看历史先例会提供很多信息。 例如，如果有人认为一项新政策会将增长率从 x 提高到 y，那么询问过去我们看到增长达到 y 的频率是一个信息丰富的练习。

反对意见2：对区间定义的敏感性

另一个对象指出，一年的间隔并没有什么特别的。 这篇文章指出，如果我们选择衡量一年、20 年或 100 多年的增长，我们会得到不同的结果。 鉴于没有理由将一个时间框架优先于另一个时间框架，我们并没有从这个练习中学到太多东西。

我不同意；较短的时间间隔之所以有用，恰恰是因为如果我们无法在非常短的时间间隔内达到给定的增长率，那么我们在较长的时间间隔内达到该增长率的可能性就较小。 想象一下，两名跑步者需要在 5 分钟内跑完 1600m 的比赛才能获得比赛资格。 如果一名跑步者至少在某些时候表现出自己能够在远低于 75 秒的时间内跑完 400m，那么他比从未在 75 秒内跑完 400m 的跑步者更有可能跑完 5 分钟一英里。

换句话说，工业革命的长期增长加速并不要求英国经济按照自己的标准达到异常快速的短期增长率，而是比以前更频繁地达到这种增长率。 今天的爆炸性增长需要达到以当代标准来看异常快的短期增长率。

结束观察

最后，我要指出的是，工业革命并不是急剧增长加速的唯一先例。 人们可以指出早期的加速，例如农业革命开始时增长率的提高，或者指出人类历史上增长加速的普遍趋势的证据。 我们没有农业革命时期的良好经济数据，因此在人类前农业时代，每年的增长不需要有太大的波动，每年超过 0.06% 的增长率是很常见的。 这意味着早期的加速度也完全位于过去观察到的分布范围内。

换句话说，正如工业革命的特点是相对常见的“好年头”变得更加普遍，“坏年头”变得不那么常见，农业革命的特点也可能是“好年头”相对于坏年头变得更加普遍。 在这两种情况下，短期增长率都不会因相对于当时的先例急剧加速而令当代观察者感到惊讶。
